## Building the Database

*Reconstructing a Hidden Archive*

How many Chinese immigrants served in the American Civil War, and what can we learn about their lives?

Attempting to answer that question required building a research database that brings together scattered historical records from multiple archives and digital collections. Because Chinese soldiers were rarely documented in a consistent way, their stories often appear only in fragments across different sources. The database was created first to help myself organize the material, and now as a way to make them easier to analyze and share.

*Identifying the Soldiers*

The first step in building the database was identifying potential Chinese soldiers in Civil War records. Fortunately, the American Battlefield Trust and the National Park Service in 2015 released a pamphlet about Asian participation in the war. In this pamphlet were lists of soldiers by name, and it was here that I began my research. After narrowing down my target list to researching Chinese soldiers serving in both the Union and the Navy, I began my work.

<p>
To identify individual soldiers, I cross-referenced records from
<a href="https://www.fold3.com/" target="_blank">Fold3</a>,
the <a href="https://catalog.archives.gov/" target="_blank">National Archives Catalog</a>,
<a href="https://www.familysearch.org/" target="_blank">FamilySearch</a>,
and other digital and archival collections.
</p>


<p>
Identifying the soldiers required tracing individuals across multiple record types,
including enlistment registers, census schedules, pension files, ship records, cemetery records,
and newspapers. In many cases, the same individual appeared under multiple spellings or different names,
which made direct identification difficult.
</p>

<p>
For example, one soldier might appear in a naval enlistment record under one spelling of his surname,
in a census under another, and in a pension index under a partially Anglicized version of his name.
<p>

(picture here demonstrating the difference in names)

Matching these records required comparing age, place of birth, service details, residence, and family connections
rather than relying on a single spelling alone.
</p> 

With this method, identifying one soldier could take hours.
